sections.heading: Should Newark Homeowners Repair or Replace the Roof Before They Install Solar Panels?

c.v: Replace the roof before solar when the covering has less remaining life than the array; repair it when the roof is young and sound.

runs.v: That is industry best practice, not a code mandate: most solar panels carry roughly 25-year performance warranties, and a roof replaced under an array forces the panels off and back on.

Architectural asphalt shingles typically last 20–30 years in Newark's climate, so a shingle roof in its mid-teens usually has less life left than a new array. Replacing an aging roof on a Newark house usually falls in the $10,000–$22,000 range, and doing it before the solar panel installation saves money by avoiding a removal and reinstallation later.

Is it a good idea to put solar panels on your roof? It can be when four things line up: a roof with more life left than the panels, enough direct sunlight, electric bills high enough to matter, and a structure that passes the load check. Urban shading complicates placement in Newark, where a taller building, a parapet, or street trees can shade a roof and change the panel layout. Rooftop solar power reduces reliance on fossil fuels and lowers carbon emissions, and sizing for future energy usage, such as an electric vehicle or a heat pump, avoids adding panels later.

When the roof under an existing array wears out, the solar installer or a New Jersey licensed electrical contractor shuts down and removes the panels, Newark Quality Roofing replaces the roof and flashes every mount point, and the installer reinstalls and recommissions the system. Get the removal-and-reinstall price in writing, and ask whether the installer's warranty term covers the penetrations it reopens.

sections.heading: What Incentives Apply to Solar in New Jersey in 2026?

c.v: Is there still a 30% solar tax credit in 2026? Not for a system a homeowner buys.

runs.v: The IRS states that the Residential Clean Energy Credit equaled 30% of the cost of qualified property installed from 2022 through December 31, 2025, and is not allowed for expenditures made after that date, which the IRS treats as made when installation is completed. Cost guides that still show a 6 kW system at about $11,676 after the credit are out of date for a 2026 install.

New Jersey solar incentives still apply in Newark. The NJ Board of Public Utilities' Successor Solar Incentive (SuSI) program creates Solar Renewable Energy Certificates (SREC-IIs) that generate income for the electricity a system produces; a May 2026 Board order kept ADI registration open until June 1, 2027 or until each capacity block fills. NJ net metering credits excess electricity against the customer's electric bills, solar energy equipment is exempt from NJ sales tax with Form ST-4, and Newark homeowners can apply for a limited property-tax exemption for a certified solar system on Form CRES.

For business-owned solar, the federal Section 48E credit ends for solar facilities placed in service after 2027 when construction began after July 4, 2026, per the IRS Form 3468 instructions. Rules for solar systems change, so NJ homeowners should confirm current programs at njcleanenergy.com and with a tax professional.

faqs.q: Do solar panel mounts leak the roof or void the roof warranty?

runs.v: Not when each attachment uses a flashed foot tucked under the upslope shingle course. Improper installation creates leak paths, and flashing that ignores the manufacturer's instructions can void the roof warranty.

faqs.q: Do you need a permit to install rooftop solar in Newark, NJ?

runs.v: Yes. A rooftop array requires an AHJ building and electrical permit and inspection; the re-roof under it on a detached one- or two-family home is ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7.

faqs.q: How long do solar panels last on a roof?

runs.v: Solar panel systems typically last 25 to 30 years, and most carry roughly 25-year performance warranties, per NREL and the DOE.

faqs.q: How does rapid shutdown work on a rooftop solar array?

runs.v: Rapid shutdown drops rooftop photovoltaic conductors to 30 volts or less outside the array boundary and 80 volts or less inside it within 30 seconds, through module-level electronics or a listed UL 3741 system.
